title: Compact LLM Proc-Fiber Architecture — personal notes
content:
Context: rough exploration of a small-footprint concurrency model for local/client-side LLM processing. Aim is to define an architecture that sits between a full actor model and a naive thread-per-request approach — think lightweight 'proc-fibers' for cooperative scheduling of small transforms, token streaming tasks, and KV cache accesses when running smaller LLMs or proxying to remote APIs.

Goals (why this exists):
- Minimize per-request memory/stack overhead on resource constrained hosts (edge devices, mobile, small containers).
- Provide predictable latency for tail-sensitive paths (first byte for streaming, quick metadata transforms).
- Allow composable chaining of small ops (tokenizer, sanitization, policy checks, prefix caches, network callouts) with backpressure and cancellation.
- Make instrumentation and sampling cheap so telemetry doesn't dominate budgets.

High level idea:
- Proc-Fiber: lightweight, heap-backed continuation object that contains only the minimal execution state and a next-step pointer. Not OS threads, not heavy coroutines with large stacks. Each proc-fiber represents a small unit of work (eg: "run tokenizer for chunk X", "apply policy policy-3", "await cache entry for prefix Y").
- Runtime scheduler keeps a few worker threads per process (configurable). Workers drive proc-fibers to completion cooperatively. When a proc-fiber needs to await I/O (disk, network, remote LLM), it yields with a compact wait token and is re-queued on completion.
- Resource accounting: per-tenant/per-request soft budgets for memory and CPU—proc-fiber allocation checks budget and can be throttled into a low-priority pool.

Primitive API shape (informal):
- spawn_fiber(parent_ctx, fiber_fn, metadata) -> fiber_id
- fiber_yield(wait_token)  // current fiber yields; runtime returns to scheduler
- resume_fiber(fiber_id, result)
- cancel_fiber(fiber_id, reason)
- fiber_inspect(fiber_id) -> {state, mem_estimate, stack_trace}

Example fiber lifecycle (text sequence):
1) Ingress thread receives request; creates request_ctx and spawns root fiber 'root:request-<id>'.
2) root fiber runs: tokenize -> sanitize -> policy-check -> decide local vs remote.
3) If local model exists and token budget permits, spawn sub-fiber 'inference-local' which will request a GPU slot or quantized executor. It yields on waiting for KV priming or GPU queue.
4) Worker threads pick up ready fibers; when remote latency finishes, resume_fiber() injects result. If result is error, root fiber can run fallback heuristics, possibly spawning 'fallback-remote' fiber.

Memory layout notes:
- Each fiber: small header (~48 bytes) + vector of small dynamic frames. Frames are tiny records describing the operation and local small values; large buffers are always heap-allocated separately and referenced by buffer_id. This avoids large implicit stacks.
- Frame design: {op_id, local_smallvals, continuation_ptr}
- Pooling: use slab allocators per-thread for frames to avoid frequent mallocs.

Backpressure and priority lanes:
- Policy: three lanes — realtime (user interactive), standard (batchy but bounded), background (best-effort). Request metadata decides lane; scheduler maintains separate queues with token-bucket enforced throughput.
- If realtime queue length passes threshold, new standard requests are either queued on a per-tenant shield or redirected to a cheaper model variant.

I/O model and wait tokens:
- Wait token = (kind, id) e.g., (NET, req-12345) or (KV, prefix-xyz) or (GPU, slot-7). Minimal 64-bit opaque value for runtime.
- On yield, fiber serializes minimal resume closure (usually a small pointer into frame array). For cross-process handoff (rare), resume closure is encoded as compact op code + ids — avoids serializing full closures.

Telemetry & sampling strategy:
- Always record fiber-level micro-metrics for a small sampled subset of requests (1% default). For all requests record only event counts and coarse timers.
- Sampling should be upstream-easy: decision made at ingress (sampled flag in request metadata) so that heavy instrumentation paths run only when requested.
- Provide cheap ‘fiber-span’ ids that can be attached to higher-level traces.

Failure modes & graceful degradation:
- If fiber pool memory pressure crosses threshold, new fibers are rejected with a typed rejection that signals the caller to fallback to remote API or degrade quality.
- Cancellation path must run a small deterministic cleanup routine (release buffer refs, decrement tenant counters); fibers should log only at low verbosity to avoid log storms.

Developer ergonomics (API ergonomics notes):
- Provide a small SDK surface for writing fiber functions in Rust/Go/Python that maps to the same primitives. For Python, fibers are thin objects with explicit yield points (not full async/await) to keep stack size tiny.
- Debugging: fiber_inspect prints a compact micro-stack: operation names, frame locals (size only), and last wait token.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to integrate with existing coroutine frameworks (tokio/async-std) without double-suspension complexity? Option: worker threads run a shim that drives both proc-fibers and native async tasks; prefer fibers for latency-sensitive routes.
- Quantify overhead vs thread-per-request for 1–8 token responses: need microbench harness. Measure throughput, cold-latency, p50/p95 for path with 3 yields.
- Security: ensure wait token space cannot be abused to coerce fibers into leaking state. Consider tenant-scoped ids and HMAC of wait token on cross-tenant handoffs.
- Persisting a fiber across process restart (session hotswap) — should be possible by writing minimal frame+wait token snapshot. Need compact serialization format.

Initial action plan (next steps):
- Spike: implement runtime core in Rust (toy) with spawn/yield/resume and a very small frame allocator.
- Microbench: compare with tokio-based prototype and with current runtime behavior for small local models.
- UX: write a 2-page explainer + sequence diagram for infra/RT/SDK integration.

Sketch: simple ASCII diagram for how fibers move between queues and workers:

  [Ingress] -> root-fiber spawn -> |Realtime Q| -> worker-1 -> executes -> yields (NET: req-42) ->
                              |                            ^                         |
                              v                            | resume_fiber on NET done   v
                         |Standard Q| -> worker-2 -> local inference fiber -> yields (GPU: slot-3)

Notes: keep this doc intentionally fuzzy; want quick iterations. Remove heavy invariants until we have bench data.
